qs.q: Before starting enteral feeding through a nasogastric tube, which verification method is recommended?
qs.e: Radiographic confirmation is the locally approved method for confirming tube placement. Auscultation after air insufflation is unreliable and not recommended.
qs.s: Nutrition and Fluid Therapy in Surgical Patients: Assessment, Feeding: MCQs

qs.q: A 60-year-old man presents with a 24-hour history of partial small bowel obstruction following an appendicectomy. He has no signs of peritonitis or strangulation. Alongside nasogastric tube decompression and IV fluids, which diagnostic and therapeutic contrast agent can be administered to assess whether the obstruction will resolve conservatively?
qs.e: A water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin) study is both diagnostic and therapeutic; if the contrast reaches the colon within 24 hours, the adhesive obstruction will usually resolve. Barium is contraindicated due to the risk of peritonitis if a leak or perforation is present.
qs.s: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome, Peritoneal Adhesions and Compartment: MCQs

qs.q: A 50-year-old man is admitted with a complete adhesive small bowel obstruction. He undergoes conservative management ('drip and suck') with a nasogastric tube and IV fluids. After how many hours of conservative treatment without clinical improvement or resolution should emergency surgery be considered mandatory?
o: 10 to 14 days of failed conservative management
12 to 24 hours of failed conservative management
5 to 7 days of failed conservative management
48 to 72 hours of failed conservative management
qs.e: Conservative management for uncomplicated partial obstruction can be trialed for 24 to 72 hours, but complete obstruction not improving or a failure of conservative treatment after 48 to 72 hours mandates emergency surgery.
qs.s: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome, Peritoneal Adhesions and Compartment: MCQs

qs.q: A term neonate presents with excessive frothy saliva from the mouth and nose shortly after birth, followed by coughing and cyanosis on attempted feeding. An 8 Fr nasogastric tube meets resistance at 11 cm. What is the most likely embryological defect responsible for this anatomical finding?
o: Failure of recanalisation of the primitive oesophagus at the 4th week
Anterior displacement of the lung buds during embryologic development
Incomplete fusion of the lateral folds of the embryonic foregut
A posterior deviation of the tracheo-oesophageal septum during development
qs.e: A posterior deviation of the tracheo-oesophageal septum produces incomplete separation of the foregut into the trachea and oesophagus, resulting in atresia with a fistula. Recanalisation failure typically occurs later at the 8th week and contributes to atresia without a fistula.
qs.s: Oesophageal Atresia and Tracheo-oesophageal Fistula: MCQs

qs.q: A newborn infant with excessive drooling of saliva undergoes insertion of an 8 Fr nasogastric tube, which coils in the upper pouch on chest X-ray. The radiograph also reveals gas within the stomach and intestinal loops. Which anatomical type of oesophageal atresia is most likely present?
qs.e: Gas in the stomach and bowel indicates a distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula connected to the lower oesophagus, which represents Type C (the commonest form). Type A features a gasless abdomen because there is no distal fistula.
qs.s: Oesophageal Atresia and Tracheo-oesophageal Fistula: MCQs

qs.q: A neonate presents with recurrent chest infections and choking on feeds, but initial routine nasogastric tube placement passed easily into the stomach without meeting resistance. Antenatal history revealed no polyhydramnios. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Pure oesophageal atresia with a long gap
Oesophageal atresia with a distal fistula
Atresia with a proximal pouch fistula
qs.e: An H-type fistula involves an isolated tracheo-oesophageal fistula without atresia, presenting later in life with recurrent respiratory symptoms rather than immediate neonatal drooling or a blocked tube. Atresia variants always prevent standard nasogastric tube passage.
qs.s: Oesophageal Atresia and Tracheo-oesophageal Fistula: MCQs

qs.q: A 50-year-old postoperative patient on enteral nutrition via a nasogastric tube develops frequent liquid stools. What is the most common gastrointestinal complication of enteral feeding experienced by this patient?
qs.e: Diarrhoea is the commonest gastrointestinal complication of enteral feeding. Constipation can occur, but diarrhoea is much more frequently cited as the primary GI complication.
qs.s: Nutritional Support in Surgical Patients: Enteral Feeding and TPN: MCQs

qs.q: A clinician passes a nasogastric tube in a patient suspected of having an upper gastrointestinal bleed. What aspirate finding makes an upper gastrointestinal source significantly less likely?
o: Bright red blood in the aspirate
qs.e: An aspirate of bile without blood makes an upper gastrointestinal bleed less likely, whereas blood or coffee-ground material supports the diagnosis.
qs.s: Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding: Peptic Ulcer and Variceal Bleeding: MCQs

es.q: Describe the diagnostic utility of nasogastric tube placement in evaluating GI bleeding and interpret the findings of the aspirate.
es.m:
- **Utility**: Initial procedure to determine if bleeding is from an upper or lower GI source and to empty the stomach to prevent aspiration.
- **Bile but no blood**: Upper GI bleeding is unlikely; source is probably distal to the ligament of Treitz.
- **Bright red blood or coffee grounds**: Indicates upper GI bleeding.
- **Non-bloody aspirate (clear fluid)**: Upper GI bleeding is unlikely but cannot be ruled out definitively.
- **False Negatives**: Possible if upper GI bleeding is intermittent or originates from a lesion in the duodenum.

ai.title: Nasogastric Tube Placement and Management
ai.subject: Surgery
ai.summary: A nasogastric tube (NGT) is used for decompression, feeding, or medication delivery. In low‑resource settings, focus on safe insertion, basic troubleshooting, and early complication recognition.

sections.p: An NGT is a flexible tube inserted through the nose, past the pharynx, into the stomach. Diagnosis of need is clinical: vomiting, ileus, aspiration risk, or need for enteral feeding.
b: Insertion is guided by patient history and bedside assessment; no imaging is required in most cases.

sections.p: NGT complications are staged by severity: minor (mucosal irritation), moderate (tube misplacement, aspiration), severe (perforation, pneumothorax).
b: Use clinical signs and simple bedside tests to stage.

sections.p: Common indications in East Africa: postoperative ileus, obstetric hemorrhage, severe vomiting, dehydration, and need for enteral nutrition.
b: Infections such as HIV or TB may delay healing; malaria can cause vomiting; herbal remedies may cause gastric irritation.

sections.p: Patients may complain of throat discomfort, nasal bleeding, or inability to swallow. Complications present as chest pain, dyspnea, or abdominal distension.
b: Look for sudden change in breathing pattern or abdominal tenderness.

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, rely on bedside tests. Imaging is reserved for suspected misplacement or perforation.

t.b: Is the patient hypoxic? – If <92% on room air, consider aspiration or pneumothorax.
Is there absent breath sounds? – Suggests pneumothorax.
Is there shifting dullness? – Indicates fluid or gas in abdomen.
Does the patient swallow saliva? – If not, tube may be in the airway.

sections.p: Immediate danger signs include sudden chest pain, severe dyspnea, or inability to pass the tube beyond 10–12 cm.
b: Pneumothorax, esophageal perforation, aspiration pneumonia, severe bleeding.

sections.p: First, confirm correct placement: auscultate over epigastrium while injecting air, or use bedside pH test of aspirate. If misplaced, reposition or replace.

t.b: Is aspirate pH <5? – Confirms gastric placement.
Does sound change from gurgle to air? – Confirms correct position.

sections.p: Monitor for tube dislodgement, maintain sterility, and educate caregivers on tube care. Replace if clogged or after 7–10 days.
b: Use a small amount of water to keep the tube patent.

sections.p: Nasogastric tube vs. nasojejunal tube (extends beyond the duodenum) and nasopharyngeal tube (used for airway suction).
b: Both start nasally but have different lengths and purposes.

sections.p: A normal pH aspirate can occur if the tube is in the distal stomach after vomiting; a low pH can be seen in gastric ulcer bleeding.
b: Always confirm with multiple tests if suspicion remains.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden chest pain or severe dyspnea
Inability to pass the tube beyond 10–12 cm
Signs of perforation (abdominal rigidity, fever, tachycardia)

faq.q: How do I confirm the tube is in the stomach?
faq.a: A bedside pH test of aspirate <5 or an air injection test with a gurgling sound over the epigastrium confirms gastric placement.

faq.q: What if the patient vomits after insertion?
faq.a: Do not induce vomiting; suction the tube, reassess placement, and consider repositioning or replacing the tube.

faq.q: Can I use the same tube for feeding and medication?
faq.a: Yes, but ensure the tube is clean and the patient is tolerating feeds; avoid large boluses that may cause aspiration.

exam: What bedside test would you use to confirm correct NGT placement? — pH <5 or air injection with gurgle; why is this preferred in low‑resource settings? — avoids imaging and is quick.
A patient develops sudden chest pain after NGT insertion. What is the most likely complication and immediate management? — pneumothorax; remove tube, call for airway support, monitor vitals.
Why is it contraindicated to induce vomiting in a patient with an NGT? — risk of tube dislodgement and aspiration; instead suction and reassess.
What are the red flags that suggest the tube is in the airway? — inability to swallow, coughing, absent breath sounds on the side of insertion.
How would you manage a clogged NGT in a setting without flushing solutions? — gently irrigate with water, rotate the tube, or replace if blockage persists.
Explain the difference between a nasogastric and a nasojejunal tube. — length and intended location; NGT ends in stomach, NJT extends beyond duodenum for distal feeding.
When should you consider imaging after NGT insertion? — if the patient shows signs of perforation, persistent vomiting, or inability to pass the tube beyond 10–12 cm.
What is the first step if a patient with an NGT develops severe abdominal distension? — decompress with the tube, give IV fluids, correct electrolytes, and monitor closely.
